Dara · 5×6 board · 12 stones each

From random moves to unbeaten in three hours

A neural network learned Dara only by playing against itself. Drag the slider to watch its score against three fixed opponents rise as the self-play games pile up.

Score = wins plus half of draws, over 32 games per opponent, measured every third training round with the network searching 100 simulations per move. The two search opponents use the same tree search with a hand-written evaluation (count the stones) instead of a network.

It kept beating its younger selves

The fixed opponents stop being informative after the first hour, because the network wins every game. Against its own earlier checkpoints, the final network still gains ground.

Final network against each checkpoint, 48 games each, both sides searching 200 simulations per move.

Three ways to learn the same game

The same network body was trained three ways on the same environment. For a like-for-like picture, every curve here is the network playing its single preferred move with no tree search, against the scripted bot that makes a three whenever it can.

How each algorithm works

Search + network · used for the main model

AlphaZero

  1. The network looks at a position and outputs two things: which moves look promising (policy) and who is winning (value).
  2. Before every move, a tree search (MCTS) plays out 200 short what-if continuations, steered by those two outputs. Moves that keep looking good get visited more.
  3. The visit counts are a better move choice than the network's first guess. The game is played with them.
  4. After the game, the network is trained to predict the search's choice and the final winner. Then repeat.

Why it works well here: the search corrects the network's mistakes immediately, so every position yields a strong training signal instead of just a win or loss at the end.

Policy gradient · no search

PPO

  1. The network outputs move probabilities and an estimate of who is winning (the critic).
  2. It plays games by sampling moves from those probabilities.
  3. For each move it asks: did things turn out better or worse than the critic expected? That difference is the advantage.
  4. Moves with positive advantage are made more likely, others less. A clip stops any single update from changing the policy by more than about 20%.

Stable and simple, but it learns only from what actually happened in its own games, and throws that data away after a few passes.

Value learning · no search

DQN

  1. The network outputs one number per move: the expected final result if I play this move and play well afterwards (the Q-value).
  2. It plays mostly its highest-rated move, sometimes a random one to explore, and stores every step in a replay buffer.
  3. Training pulls each Q-value towards "reward now, plus the best Q-value of the next position", negated when the opponent moves next.
  4. A frozen copy of the network supplies those targets and is refreshed periodically, to keep training stable.

Reuses old data well, but in Dara the only reward is the result after roughly 90 actions, so the signal has to seep backwards one step at a time.
